title: Are You My Fan
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece uses the psychology of sports fandom to reframe how leaders should relate to their own team members. Fans cheer loyally regardless of the score, and their enthusiasm creates a measurable home-field advantage for performers, the piece argues leaders can create the same effect. Importantly, the piece separates being a fan from being an uncritical cheerleader: great leaders can be unabashed fans while still holding people accountable. The payoff described is reciprocal, team members who know their leader is truly in their corner work harder to justify that support.
points: Fandom creates a documented performance boost, and the piece argues leaders can replicate that effect by becoming genuine fans of their own team.
Being a fan of your team members is compatible with, not opposed to, holding them accountable.
Team members who feel unconditionally supported by a leader-as-fan gain the confidence to perform.
The relationship is framed as reciprocal: fans make the star, and the star performs in a way that rewards the fans' belief.
quotes: Unless they represent the fair-weather version, fans are loyal and root for those they admire no matter what the score or social acclaim.
Home court or home-field advantage illustrates the power a stadium of fans can have on performance.
Great leaders are great fans of those they lead. They would do anything for team members to succeed.
Being a fan doesn’t mean leaders don’t hold others accountable or refrain from delivering a tough message.
Fans make the star and the star shines for its fans. What a great relationship.
